name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is a compiled systems language first released in 1985, standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21, and it is the performance layer underneath most AI work: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and many inference runtimes are written in it. A developer deciding whether to use it should know that it buys speed and memory control at the cost of manual complexity, and that it is usually paired with Python rather than replacing it.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled, statically typed programming language whose first release was in 1985, maintained through the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee and documented at isocpp.org. It sits at the performance layer of the AI stack, underneath the Python surface that most practitioners touch. PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++, so when a model trains or a request is served, C++ is frequently doing the work even when the user's code is Python. The official site frames this as a language for operating under real space and time constraints, and its standardization blog tracks work on C++26 and C++29 features such as reflection, std::simd, std::execution and memory safety profiles.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete AI jobs C++ does are training and inference engines, data pipelines, serving runtimes and edge deployment, because those are the places where latency, throughput and memory footprint are decided. The site's own material points to inference runtimes and framework cores as the load-bearing examples, and to std::simd and std::execution as standard library performance enhancers arriving in C++26. It is strongest where a Python prototype has hit a wall and the hot path must be rewritten, or where a model must run on constrained hardware. It is not the first choice for exploratory notebook work, where Python remains the natural surface.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: C++ has a reputation for a steep learning curve, and the official site does not pretend otherwise. It is now more than 45 years since the language was first conceived, and the standardization blog shows a steady stream of new papers, so the language keeps moving. Prerequisites are real: some systems knowledge such as memory layout and compilation, and enough mathematics to follow the numerical code you intend to write. The official site is primarily a hub for standards news, papers, meeting minutes and the annual developer survey rather than a tutorial, so a beginner should expect to learn from books, courses and compiler documentation, and to treat isocpp.org as the place to follow where the language is going.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around C++ is large and standards driven. The site documents regular mailings of new standards papers, working group minutes for SG14 on low latency, games, embedded and financial trading, and SG19 on machine learning, plus trip reports from ISO meetings in Kona, Varna and Brno. Compiler support is tracked in detail, for example GCC 16.1 shipping C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening with C++20 enabled by default. Conferences such as CppCon, held in Aurora, Colorado, and community events such as Meeting C++ with Herb Sutter, are promoted on the site, and the annual global developer survey, a ten minute exercise, feeds results back to the committee and to tool vendors.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for production performance rather than quick experiments. The site's framing is explicit: it is a language for operating under real space and time constraints, and the C++26 additions of std::simd and std::execution are aimed at making that performance easier to reach. The cost is that the same control which delivers speed also demands care, since memory management, build configuration and undefined behavior are the programmer's responsibility. The committee is addressing that cost directly, with an Annex in the C++29 working draft cataloging every case of core language undefined behavior and draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety now being prototyped. For fast iteration, most teams prototype in Python and move the hot path into C++.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: C++ is a current standard, not a legacy choice, and it is used wherever AI systems must run efficiently. The site cites industry data from SlashData and IDC documenting sustained growth in demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints, and it notes that the ISO committee completed technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and voted the first C++29 additions in June 2026. For someone choosing what to learn, that means C++ skills remain relevant to inference, serving, robotics and edge work, though the site does not publish specific salary or hiring figures, so those questions are left to other sources.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: C++ is typically used with Python rather than against it. The common polyglot pattern is Python for orchestration, data preparation and experimentation, with C++ underneath in framework cores, custom operators, CUDA kernels and inference runtimes, and with bindings such as pybind11 or libtorch connecting the two. It also sits beside CUDA for GPU work and beside Rust in conversations about safety, a comparison the site touches on in a CppCon talk about JSON serialization performance. The site does not present C++ as a replacement for Python in AI work, and the facts it holds describe it as the performance layer beneath the Python surface.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: C++ is weak where rapid iteration and safety by default matter most, and the committee's own agenda acknowledges this through its work on undefined behavior, safety profiles and contracts. Those efforts are still in progress: the undefined behavior catalog and the memory safety profiles target C++29, and GCC's C++20 modules support remains experimental behind a flag. The official site does not say how quickly profiles will be adopted by compilers or vendors, does not give benchmarks comparing C++ with Python or Rust for AI workloads, and does not offer a beginner curriculum. A blog post on the site also illustrates a practical caution about AI generated code review, noting that a model reported zero-length bugs in a C++ library that a human then had to verify.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
